sections.heading: Abstract
sections.text:
Electro-reduction of carbon dioxide (CO2) is a promising way to curb the excessive CO2 emission and produce value-added products. Gold-copper (AuCu) alloys are known to exhibit
eminent CO production performance towards CO2ER. However, it still remains a grand challenge to balance *COOH and *CO bonding and to further descend CO onset potential. This
paper describes the construction of Cu vacancies at an abrupt surface over a dealloyed AuCu
catalyst to effectively decrease the overpotential and increase CO faradaic efficiency. Dealloyed
Au3Cu exhibited a 90.2% CO faradaic efficiency at -0.38 V vs. RHE and a 418.60 A/g CO mass current density at -0.8 V. vs RHE, achieving the record for CO production among AuCu catalysts.
Combined with experimental and theoretical results, we concluded that the improved
performance primarily results from the enhanced *COOH absorption.

Electrochemical conversion of CO2 to value-added products is a significant route to curb the excessive CO2 emission and alleviate corresponding problems such as “Greenhouse effect” 1-2 . Due to the eminent conductivity and the adjustable intermediate bonding, metal catalysts have been widely investigated 3-10 . Among them, Au has been proved to be the most optimal catalyst for CO production 11-13 . Various routes have been applied to further optimize the intermediate adsorption energy and reactive activities of Au. Construction on Au composition 14-16 , size 17 , facets 12 , oxidative states 11 , and even field-induced reagent concentration 13 could availably
promote CO formation. Therein, compositional adjustment is proved to be an effective way, as it could greatly influence the intermediate adsorption via electronic effect 16 . Besides, non-noble
metal adding could keep the catalyst cost down, being beneficial to wider application of Au in

sections.heading: CO2ER.
sections.text:
Due to the stronger intermediate bonding, Cu has always been incorporated to improve the
bonding ability of Au. For example, Yang et.al use uniform AuxCuy nanoparticles with different compositions to adjust *COOH and *CO adsorption energy. They found Au3Cu exhibited the most optimal CO production performance, with ~63% CO faradaic efficiency at -0.73 V vs. RHE 16 . Kim et.al fabricated Au thin layer on Cu polycrystalline surface via electrochemical
galvanic displacement, achieving a CO faradaic efficiency 3.4 times higher than that of polycrystalline Au 18 Despite of the great progress in promoting CO production, it’s still a huge
challenge to further descend the CO onset potential and increase CO faradaic efficiency.
It has been reported that introducing metal vacancy defects into catalytic surface could
effectively alter the reactive pathway and product distribution, as it could effectively influence the electronic structure of neighbouring atoms and thus change the reactive energy barrier 15, 19-20 .
Li et.al synthesized jagged Platinum nanowires through Pt/Ni dealloying, enabling high mass

activity towards oxygen reduction reaction 21
. Zhuang et al. found that by structuring a Cu2S core
with Cu surface vacancies, *C2H3O would be more easier to generate C2 liquid product 19 . Therefore, it could be speculated that the introduced vacancy defects on AuCu alloy through
dealloying would also significantly influence the *COOH or *CO adsorption energy and the CO
production performance.
This paper describes the catalyst with enriched defects at an abrupt Au (100) surface via
dealloyed Au3Cu nanocubes (De-Au3Cu) towards CO2ER. De-Au3Cu exhibited an apparently decreased CO onset potential and enhanced CO faradaic efficiencies. The maximum CO faradaic
efficiency of 94.3% and a CO current density of 48.6 A/g were achieved at -0.43 V vs. RHE in
CO2 saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 aqueous solution. Additionally, its performance remained unchanged after an over 30-hours stability test. The enhanced performance was attributed to the
enriched defects at Au surfaces, which could effectively enhance the *COOH absorption.
Due to the eminent performance of Au (100) facets for CO production 12 , we employed
Au3Cu nanocubes as the initial catalysts. According to a slightly modified recipe 22 , one pot synthesis of Au3Cu nanocubes employed gold chloride trihydrite and copper acetylacetonate as metal sources, solvents (1-dodecanethiol, diphenyl ether) as reductants and capping agents, with
the assistance of 1-adamantanecarboxylic acid, 1,2-hexadecanediol and 1-hexadecylamine. Then
Au3Cu nanocubes were treated with acid (acetic acid or nitric acid) for different duration to etch surficial Cu atoms away, denoted as De-Au3Cu. Before dealloying, high resolution transmission electronmicroscopy (HRTEM) image and fast Fourier transform (FFT) (Figure S1) exhibited the
perfect atomic arrangement and crystal lattice, without any defects. Lattice distance of 0.201 nm corresponds to the interplanar distance of Au3Cu (200) facets 23 . Energy-dispersive (EDS) mapping profile shows the uniform distribution of elemental Au and Cu in nanocubes (Figure

S1). Figure S2 shows atomic ratio of De-Au3Cu (treated with acetic acid for 5hrs), with 81.4 : 18.6 of Au : Cu, slightly larger than precursor ratio. Figure 1a shows that dealloyed Au3Cu nanocubes exhibit the uniform morphology, with edge length around 20 nm. Dashed yellow
circles in HRTEM of Figure 1b clearly exhibits atomic vacancies and defects on surficial Au
atoms. EDS line mapping profiles (Figure 1c) show the absence of Cu in shell and thickness of
Au shell is measured to be around 0.56 nm (2-3 atomic layers). Besides, it’s reported that three atomic Au layers over the AuCu alloy core stayed efficient and stable during CO2ER test 22 . Thus we consider De-Au3Cu (treated with acetic acid for 5 hrs) as Au3Cu@Au structure.
To further confirm the De-Au3Cu structure, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was used to characterize the surficial composition and structure. As shown in Figure 1d, the peak of
Au3Cu nanocubes in Cu 2p XPS spectrum at around 931.8 eV and 952.1 eV can be assigned to Cu(I)/Cu(0) species, and the peak at 934.6 eV and 943.8 eV can be assigned to Cu (II),
suggesting partial Cu oxidation on surface. It could be explained that when exposed to air,
surface Cu atoms are easily to be oxidized while subsurface Cu tend to maintain metallic states.
For De-Au3Cu, the peak at 934.6 eV obviously weakens and the peak at 943.8 eV almost disappeared, further indicating the disappearance of surficial Cu atoms 24 . The slight shifts in
binding energies of AuCu compared to pure Au (Figure S3) and Cu (Figure 1e) suggest the
strong electronic interaction between Au and Cu, confirming AuCu alloy structure. We then
determined the crystalline structure of Au (TEM images shown in Figure S4), Au3Cu and DeAu3Cu by X-Ray Diffraction (XRD). Diffraction peaks of Au (111) at 38.18° can be observed over Au nanocubes. For Au3Cu and De-Au3Cu samples, peaks corresponding to (111) shift to higher angles, indicating the decrease of interplanar spacing with Cu atoms replacing Au atoms and the Au–Cu alloy forming (Figure 1e) 25 . Magnified XRD (Figure 1f) shows that peaks of

Au3Cu-1 (treated with acetic acid for 5 hrs) stays unchanged compared to Au3Cu, while that of Au3Cu-2 (treated with nitric acid for 30 min) shows a negative shift. It could be understood that the nitric acid owns much stronger oxidative ability than acetic acid. Thus acetic acid only etched
surficial Cu atoms away mildly, while nitric acid quickly reacts with both surficial and inner Cu
atoms. Consequently, Au3Cu-1 treated with acetic acid remained similar XRD patterns as untreated Au3Cu, while Au3Cu-2 treated with nitric acid behaved like pure Au in XRD spectra. Figure S5 shows TEM images of Au3Cu-2, with lattice distance of 0.235 nm, corresponding to Au (111) facets,and is in accordance with XRD patterns.
Additionally, the electrochemical character of catalysts was compared. Electrochemical active
surface area (ECSA) was tested via underpotential-deposited desorption method (Figure 2a) 13 . De-Au3Cu nanocubes exhibit the ECSA of 29.4 m 2 /g, larger than 25.1 m 2 /g of Au3Cu (Figure 2b). Due to their nearly equal size, we consider that the enlarged ECSA of De-Au3Cu results from surficial defects and roughness. To measure the charge transfer resistance (Rct) for
catalysts, we performed electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) at -0.43 V. Our
experimental results (Figure 2c) suggest a smaller charge transfer resistance of De-Au3Cu, correlating to faster electron transfer from the catalyst surface to the reactant 26 . Moreover, to
investigate on the kinetics factors over catalysts, Tafel plots are shown in Figure 2d. It has been
reported that the Tafel slope of 60 mV/dec indicates a fast equilibrium process for CO2 protonation and 120 mV/dec indicates it a rate-determining process 13 . Additionally, a smaller Tafel slope means a similar potential change would drive a larger current increase 11, 27 . The Tafel
slope of De-Au3Cu is 58.1 mV/dec, similar to 66.3 mV/dec of Au3Cu and much less than 101.5 mV/dec of Au. Thus we could conclude that De-Au3Cu perform the most favorable kinetics for CO2 protonation.

CO2ER performance tests are performed in a two-compartment batch cell with a common three-electrode system. CO2 saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 aqueous solution is employed as electrolyte. Linear sweep voltammetry (Figure 3a) suggest that De-Au3Cu (treated with acetic acid for 5hrs) exhibits the lowest overpotential, followed by Au and then Au3Cu. Additionally, De-Au3Cu shows larger current densities under the whole potential range. On-line micro gas
chromatography is responsible for products detection. Monoxide (CO) and hydrogen (H2) are two major products. De-Au3Cu achieved CO faradaic efficiency of 90.2% at -0.38 V vs. RHE and then achieved maximum CO faradaic efficiency of 94.3% at -0.43 V (Figure 3b). Its
performance exceeds all of the current AuCu nanocatalysts for CO2ER (Figure S6). Compared to De-Au3Cu, Au and Au3Cu achieve maximum CO faradaic efficiencies at more negative cathode potentials, with 85.9% at -0.7 V and 47.8% at -0.8 V, respectively. Figure 3c shows CO mass
current densities, De-Au3Cu exhibits 418.6 A/g CO mass current density at -0.8 V, far exceeding 235.7 A/g of Au and 98.4 A/g of Au3Cu. H2 production exhibits the opposite trend that DeAu3Cu produces comparatively little H2 under the whole potential range from -0.38 V to -0.8 V (Figure S7a). And H2 mass current density was inhibited below 20 A/g at -0.8 V (Figure S7b). Additionally, H2 and CO geometric current densities were shown in Figure S8. De-Au3Cu exhibits CO geometric current densities over 40 mA/cm 2 and H2 geometric current densities less than 2 mA/cm 2 at -0.8 V. The CO2ER performance of differently treated Au3Cu was shown in Figure S9. When Au3Cu nanocubes were treated with nitric acid for 30 min, only 19.7% CO faradaic efficiency was achieved at -0.43 V, as the excessive dealloying etches nearly all the Cu
atoms away and destroys cube-like morphology of Au3Cu. Finally, we conducted stability test on De-Au3Cu with acetic acid for 5 hrs. The experiment was performed at -0.38 V in 0.5 M KHCO3 aqueous solution. A total current density around 3 mA/cm 2 and CO faradaic efficiency over 90%

remained stable over 30 hrs (Figure 3d). Figure S10 shows that De-Au3Cu nanocubes after reaction remained cube-like morphology and enriched surficial defects. XPS spectra (Figure S11)
how almost the same peak position of De-Au3Cu compared to that before dealloying. These results indicate the stable morphology and composition of De-Au3Cu enables the eminent stability of CO2ER performance.
To further elucidate the mechanism of improved CO2ER performance on De-Au3Cu, we performed density functional theory (DFT) calculations via computational hydrogen electrode
(CHE) model. CO2ER is known to consist of three steps (Figure 4a). The first step is CO2 molecules absorbs on surface and protonate to *COOH, the second step is *COOH conversion to *CO, and the last step is *CO desorption from surface 28-29 . It has been reported that *COOH conversion to *CO is a thermodynamically downhill process 30 . Therefore we only consider *COOH absorption and *CO desorption process 31-34
. DFT models of Au (100), Au3Cu (100),
Au3Cu + Au (100) and De-Au3Cu (100) are presented in Figure S12. Therein, the outlayer of Au3Cu (100) consists of both Au and Cu atoms; while the outlayer of Au3Cu + Au (100) and DeAu3Cu (100) consists of only Au atoms. According to the DFT results, the free energy of CO2 absorption and its protonation to *COOH on near vacancies of De-Au3Cu (100) is 1.04 eV, which is much lower than that of Au3Cu + Au (100) (Table S1). Therefore, we consider that CO2 would be much easier to adsorb on vacancies rather than on other metal sites. When a vacancy
(the red circle marked in Figure 4a and Figure S12) exists on De-Au3Cu (100), both *COOH and *CO absorb on the atom near the vacancy. As is shown in Figure 4b, Au exhibits the weak *CO
adsorption, as its *CO desorption is a thermodynamically downhill process. However, it needs a
free energy of 1.48 eV for Au to absorb *COOH, indicating an extremely difficult process for Au
to achieve *COOH absorption. On the contrary, although Au3Cu and De-Au3Cu all need to

9
overcome an energy barrier around 0.2 eV for CO desorption, they exhibit relatively strong
ability of *COOH absorption. Among them, the energy barrier for *COOH absorption of De-
Au3Cu is 0.24 eV lower than that of Au3Cu. Meanwhile, their energy barrier for *CO desorption and *H absorption (Figure 4c) is quite similar. Therefore, we could conclude that De-Au3Cu exhibit the most optimal CO production performance towards CO2ER.
By acid treatment on Au3Cu nanocubes to etch Cu atoms away, enriched vacancies and defects are created on the surface. *COOH absorption is significantly enhanced on De-Au3Cu. Therefore, CO2ER performance on De-Au3Cu is significantly enhanced, exhibiting a much positive onset potential for CO production and improved CO faradaic efficiency of 94.3% at -0.43 VRHE. Both geometric current density and CO faradaic efficiency remained stable at an over 30 hrs
electrochemical stability test. DFT result suggests that De-Au3Cu exhibits much stronger *COOH adsorption than Au3Cu and Au, while it maintains slightly weaker *CO adsorption than Au3Cu, which contribute to the enhanced CO production performance of De-Au3Cu. To sum up, dealloying provides a promising way for introducing vacancies and adjusting the intermediate
bonding to promote CO production towards CO2ER.
